subject: Business
title: Push vs. Pull Supply Chains
description: Learn Push vs. Pull Supply Chains in one minute.

hook.text: A supermarket stocks 50,000 items hoping you'll buy some. That's push. Toyota builds a car only after you order it.

buildup.text: Push systems produce based on forecasts. Pull systems produce based on actual demand.

discovery.text: Push risks overproduction and waste. Pull risks delays and stockouts if production can't keep up.

twist.text: Most real supply chains are hybrid: push for stable items, pull for customizable or volatile ones.

climax.text: Dell revolutionized PCs with a pull model: build-to-order eliminated billions in unsold inventory.

punchline.text: Push guesses what you'll want. Pull waits until you tell it.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between push and pull supply chains?
options: Push produces based on forecasts; pull produces based on actual demand
Push is faster; pull is cheaper
Push uses trucks; pull uses ships

details.summary: Push supply chains produce and distribute goods based on demand forecasts before customer orders arrive, while pull systems only produce and move goods in response to actual customer demand. Most modern supply chains use a hybrid push-pull strategy with a decoupling point.
details.whyItMatters: Choosing between push and pull strategies fundamentally shapes inventory levels, responsiveness, and cost structure. The optimal approach depends on demand predictability, product customization, and acceptable lead times.
takeaways: Push strategies pre-build inventory based on forecasts for fast delivery
Pull strategies respond to actual demand, reducing inventory waste
The decoupling point marks where push transitions to pull in hybrid systems

faq.question: What determines where to place the push-pull decoupling point?
faq.answer: Products with predictable demand and long production times push inventory close to customers. Products with variable demand or high customization pull from earlier stages. The decoupling point balances forecast accuracy against customer lead time expectations.

faq.question: Can you give examples of push versus pull supply chains?
faq.answer: Grocery stores use push systems, stocking shelves based on forecasts. Dell historically used pull, building computers only after customer orders. Amazon uses hybrid approaches, pre-positioning popular items nearby while dropshipping slower-moving products from suppliers.
